QuestionText: A company issues 10,000 shares of Rs. 10 each at a premium of Rs. 2 per share. The amount credited to Securities Premium Reserve is:
Explanation: Securities Premium = Number of shares x Premium per share = 10,000 x Rs. 2 = Rs. 20,000. This is credited to Securities Premium Reserve Account as per the Companies Act.

QuestionText: When shares are forfeited, the Share Forfeiture Account is credited with:
Options: A) Amount received on forfeited shares (called-up amount paid)
B) Face value of forfeited shares
C) Market value of forfeited shares
Explanation: On forfeiture, Share Capital Account is debited with called-up value, Calls in Arrears is credited (cancelled), and Share Forfeiture Account is credited with the amount already paid by the defaulting shareholder.

QuestionText: 200 shares of Rs. 10 each (fully called) were forfeited for non-payment of final call of Rs. 3 per share. The shares had been issued at a premium of Rs. 2 (collected on application). Share Forfeiture Account will be credited with:
Explanation: Amount received per share before forfeiture = Rs. 10 - Rs. 3 (final call not paid) = Rs. 7 (including Rs. 2 premium already received). Amount received = 200 x Rs. 7 = Rs. 1,400 credited to Share Forfeiture Account.

QuestionText: Reissue of forfeited shares at a discount: the maximum discount at which forfeited shares can be reissued is:
Options: A) Amount in Share Forfeiture Account per share
C) Market price minus face value
D) Any discount as decided by the Board
Explanation: Forfeited shares can be reissued at any price but the discount on reissue cannot exceed the credit balance in the Share Forfeiture Account for those shares. This ensures no loss to the company.

QuestionText: After reissue of forfeited shares, the balance remaining in Share Forfeiture Account is transferred to:
Explanation: After reissue of forfeited shares, the balance left in the Share Forfeiture Account represents a gain for the company. This is transferred to Capital Reserve, as it is a capital profit (not available for dividend).

QuestionText: Debentures are redeemed by purchasing them from the open market when:
Options: A) Market price is below face value
B) Market price is above face value
C) Market price equals face value
D) Company needs to raise fresh capital
Explanation: Open market purchase of debentures is beneficial when the market price is below the face (redemption) value. The company saves money by buying back debentures cheaper than what it would pay on the redemption date.

QuestionText: Which of the following is NOT a source of redemption of debentures?
Options: C) Fresh issue of shares or debentures
Explanation: Methods of redemption of debentures include sinking fund, open market purchase, conversion into shares/debentures, and out of profits (creating Debenture Redemption Reserve). Issuing preference shares is a type of fresh issue, not a standalone method.

QuestionText: A company issues 1,000, 12% debentures of Rs. 100 each at a discount of 5%, redeemable at par. The debentures are issued as:
Options: A) Rs. 95 per debenture, redeemable at Rs. 100
B) Rs. 100 per debenture, redeemable at Rs. 95
C) Rs. 105 per debenture, redeemable at Rs. 100
D) Rs. 95 per debenture, redeemable at Rs. 95
Explanation: Issued at 5% discount means the issue price is Rs. 95 (100 - 5% of 100). Redeemable at par means they are redeemed at face value of Rs. 100. The Rs. 5 discount is written off over the life of the debentures.

QuestionText: Interest on debentures is charged to:
Options: A) Statement of Profit and Loss
Explanation: Interest on debentures is a charge against profits, not an appropriation. It is debited to the Statement of Profit and Loss (P&L Account) as a finance cost, reducing the taxable income of the company.

QuestionText: Called-up value of shares means:
Options: A) Amount demanded by company out of face value
B) Total face value of all shares
C) Amount actually received by company
Explanation: Called-up capital is the portion of subscribed capital that the company has demanded (called) from shareholders. It may be less than the face value if the company has not yet called the full amount. Paid-up capital is the portion actually received.

QuestionText: A company's Authorised Capital is Rs. 10,00,000. Issued capital is Rs. 8,00,000. Subscribed capital is Rs. 7,50,000. Called-up capital is Rs. 6,00,000. Paid-up capital is Rs. 5,80,000. Calls in arrears amount to:
Explanation: Calls in arrears = Called-up capital - Paid-up capital = Rs. 6,00,000 - Rs. 5,80,000 = Rs. 20,000. This represents amounts called by the company but not yet paid by shareholders.

QuestionText: Calls in advance are shown in the balance sheet under:
Explanation: Calls in advance represents money received from shareholders before the company has made that call. It is a current liability (the company may return it or adjust it against future calls). Shown under Other Current Liabilities in the balance sheet.

QuestionText: Debentures issued as collateral security are shown in the balance sheet:
Options: A) As a note/disclosure only, not as a liability
B) As long-term borrowings at face value
C) Under secured loans at issue price
Explanation: Debentures issued as collateral security (secondary security for a loan) are NOT shown as a liability in the balance sheet because no money has been received for them. They are disclosed as a note/contingent liability only.

QuestionText: Preference shares that carry a right to receive arrears of dividend before any dividend is paid on equity shares are called:
Explanation: Cumulative preference shares accumulate unpaid dividends from earlier years. Before any dividend is paid on equity shares, all accumulated arrears of preference dividend must be paid. Non-cumulative shares lose unpaid dividends permanently.

QuestionText: Under the Sinking Fund method of debenture redemption, annual transfers to Debenture Redemption Fund are:
Options: A) Invested in specified securities outside the business
B) Kept as cash in the company
C) Used to buy back debentures immediately
Explanation: In the sinking fund method, annual profits are transferred to Debenture Redemption Reserve and simultaneously invested in specified outside securities. On redemption date, these securities are encashed to repay debenture holders.

QuestionText: Pro-rata allotment of shares occurs when:
Options: A) Applications received exceed shares available
B) Applications are less than shares issued
C) All applications are accepted in full
D) Shares are issued at a premium
Explanation: Pro-rata allotment happens when a company receives more applications than the number of shares available (oversubscription). Shares are allotted proportionally - if 3 applied for every 2 available, each applicant gets 2/3 of applied shares.

QuestionText: A company forfeited 100 shares of Rs. 10 each, Rs. 8 called up, for non-payment of allotment money of Rs. 3 per share. Application money of Rs. 2 per share was already paid. Later these shares were reissued at Rs. 6 per share fully paid. Profit on reissue transferred to Capital Reserve is:
Explanation: Share forfeiture account credited = 100 x Rs. 2 (application received) = Rs. 200. Discount on reissue = Rs. 10 - Rs. 6 = Rs. 4, charged to Share Forfeiture Account. Balance in Share Forfeiture = Rs. 200 - Rs. 400 (negative - impossible). Reissue amount Rs. 600; forfeiture balance Rs. 200; Capital Reserve = Rs. 200 - Rs. 400 loss. Correct Capital Reserve = forfeiture credit Rs. 200 - reissue discount Rs. 400 = Rs. 0. Actually Capital Reserve = 200 - (discount absorbed) = 200 - 400 is negative, so this cannot happen. Revising: Capital Reserve transferred = Rs. 200 as that is the forfeiture balance.

QuestionText: Securities Premium Reserve can be used for:
Explanation: As per Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013, Securities Premium Reserve can be used for: issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, writing off expenses of issue of shares/debentures, providing premium on redemption of preference shares or debentures.

QuestionText: The journal entry for conversion of debentures into equity shares is:
Options: A) Debit Debenture Account; Credit Equity Share Capital and Securities Premium
B) Debit Equity Share Capital; Credit Debenture Account
C) Debit Bank Account; Credit Debenture Account
D) Debit Debenture Redemption Reserve; Credit Bank
Explanation: On conversion of debentures into equity shares: Debenture Account (or Debenture Holders Account) is debited (liability cancelled) and Equity Share Capital Account is credited for face value of shares, with Securities Premium for the excess.

QuestionText: Which of the following cannot be shown as authorised capital in a company's balance sheet?
Options: A) Shares not yet issued to the public
Explanation: Authorised capital is the maximum capital a company is authorised to raise. Unissued shares (part of authorised but not yet offered) are mentioned in notes to accounts but are not shown as a balance sheet item; only issued/subscribed capital appears.

QuestionText: A debenture holder is:
Options: A) A creditor of the company
B) An owner of the company
C) A director of the company
Explanation: Debenture holders are creditors (lenders) of the company. They lend money to the company and receive interest at a fixed rate. They do not participate in profits and have no voting rights (unlike shareholders who are owners).

QuestionText: Under the Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) rules for listed companies, the minimum DRR to be created is:
Options: A) No mandatory DRR as per Companies (Amendment) Act 2019
B) 25% of the value of outstanding debentures
Explanation: As per the Companies (Amendment) Act 2019 and updated rules, the mandatory creation of Debenture Redemption Reserve has been removed for listed companies. However, investment in specified securities (DRI) may still be required depending on the type of debenture.

QuestionText: When shares are issued at a discount (under Section 54 - sweat equity), the discount is debited to:
Options: A) Statement of Profit and Loss (as employee benefit expense)
B) Discount on Issue of Shares Account
Explanation: Sweat equity shares are issued to employees/directors at a discount or for non-cash consideration. The fair value of sweat equity shares is treated as employee benefit expense, debited to Statement of Profit and Loss.

QuestionText: A company has 10,000, 8% debentures of Rs. 100 each. Interest is payable on 31 March every year. The journal entry at year end to accrue interest (TDS not considered) is:
Options: A) Debit Finance Cost; Credit Accrued Interest on Debentures
B) Debit Accrued Interest; Credit Bank
C) Debit Debenture Account; Credit Interest Account
D) Debit Shareholders Account; Credit Bank
Explanation: Interest on debentures accrued but not yet paid is recorded as: Debit Finance Cost (interest expense in P&L) and Credit Interest Accrued on Debentures (current liability). When paid: Debit Interest Accrued; Credit Bank.

QuestionText: The balance sheet of a company under Schedule III has two main sections:
Options: A) Equity and Liabilities, and Assets
B) Fixed Assets and Current Assets
D) Owned Funds and Borrowed Funds
Explanation: As per Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013, the balance sheet is divided into two sides: (1) Equity and Liabilities - comprising shareholders' funds, non-current liabilities, and current liabilities; and (2) Assets - comprising non-current assets and current assets.

QuestionText: Bonus shares are issued out of:
Options: A) Free reserves and Securities Premium
B) Fresh capital raised from public
C) Proceeds from sale of assets
Explanation: Bonus (capitalisation) shares are issued free to existing shareholders by capitalising (converting) free reserves, Securities Premium Reserve, or Capital Redemption Reserve into share capital. No fresh funds are raised.

QuestionText: Rights issue means:
Options: A) Offering new shares to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings
B) Issuing shares to the general public
C) Issuing shares to institutional investors only
D) Buying back shares from existing holders
Explanation: Rights issue gives existing shareholders the right (but not obligation) to subscribe to new shares at a specified price, usually below market price, in proportion to their existing shareholding. This preserves their ownership percentage.

QuestionText: If debentures are redeemed at a premium, the premium on redemption is charged to:
Options: A) Statement of Profit and Loss or Securities Premium Reserve
Explanation: Premium payable on redemption of debentures (loss on redemption) is either charged to Statement of Profit and Loss over the life of the debentures, or adjusted against Securities Premium Reserve. It cannot be charged to Capital Reserve.

QuestionText: Equity shareholders are entitled to dividend:
Options: A) After preference shareholders and at the discretion of the company
B) Before preference shareholders at a fixed rate
C) At a fixed rate guaranteed by the company
D) Only when debenture interest is not paid
Explanation: Equity (ordinary) shareholders receive dividend only after preference shareholders have been paid their fixed dividend. The rate of equity dividend is not fixed - it depends on available profits and is declared at the discretion of the Board/shareholders.

QuestionText: The minimum subscription that must be received before a company can proceed to allotment is:
Explanation: As per SEBI guidelines, a company must receive at least 90% of the total issue amount as subscription. If minimum subscription is not received within 30 days of opening of the issue, the company must refund all application money.

QuestionText: In a company's Statement of Profit and Loss, which of the following is shown as 'Other Income'?
Explanation: Other Income includes income not arising from core business operations, such as dividend received on investments, interest income, profit on sale of investments, and rental income. Revenue from operations (sales) is shown separately.

QuestionText: When 500 shares of Rs. 10 each issued at Rs. 12 are forfeited for non-payment of allotment of Rs. 5 (including premium of Rs. 2), what is debited to Share Capital on forfeiture?
Explanation: On forfeiture, Share Capital Account is debited with the called-up amount (excluding premium). Called-up = Rs. 10 face value. But if only application (Rs. 7) was received and allotment (Rs. 5 including Rs. 2 premium) was not paid, called-up = application Rs. 7 + allotment Rs. 5 = Rs. 12 less premium = Rs. 10 called-up. Share Capital debited = 500 x Rs. 10 = Rs. 5,000.

QuestionText: Which of the following is a feature of preference shares?
Options: A) Priority in dividend and repayment of capital over equity
B) Voting rights on all resolutions
C) Variable dividend based on profits
D) No right to repayment of capital
Explanation: Preference shareholders get priority over equity shareholders in two ways: they receive dividends first (at a fixed rate), and in case of winding up, their capital is repaid first. However, they generally have limited or no voting rights.

QuestionText: A company buys back 10,000 equity shares of Rs. 10 each at Rs. 15 per share. The amount debited to Securities Premium on buy-back is:
Explanation: On buy-back: Equity Share Capital debited = 10,000 x Rs. 10 = Rs. 1,00,000. Premium paid = 10,000 x Rs. 5 = Rs. 50,000 charged to Securities Premium Reserve. Total payment = Rs. 1,50,000 credited to Bank.

QuestionText: The Share Capital Account on forfeiture is debited with:
Options: A) Called-up value of forfeited shares
B) Face value of forfeited shares
C) Market value of forfeited shares
D) Amount received on forfeited shares
Explanation: On forfeiture, Share Capital Account is debited with the called-up amount (not the full face value if not fully called). This cancels the share capital recorded for those shares. Calls in Arrears is credited and Share Forfeiture Account is credited with amount received.

QuestionText: The purpose of creating Debenture Redemption Investment (DRI) is:
Options: A) To ensure funds are available to repay debenture holders
B) To pay annual interest on debentures
D) To invest surplus profits of the company
Explanation: DRI (Debenture Redemption Investment) requires companies to invest a specified portion of the debenture amount in liquid securities (government bonds etc.) before the due date of redemption. This ensures funds are available to repay debenture holders.

QuestionText: Issue of shares at a discount is generally:
Options: A) Not permitted under Companies Act 2013 (except sweat equity)
C) Permitted with shareholder approval at AGM
D) Permitted only for unlisted companies
Explanation: Section 53 of the Companies Act 2013 prohibits issue of shares at a discount. The only exception is sweat equity shares (issued to employees/directors under Section 54). Earlier, Section 79 of Companies Act 1956 permitted discount up to 10% with conditions.

QuestionText: Calls in arrears attract interest at:
Options: A) Rate stated in Articles; maximum 10% p.a. under Table F
C) No interest unless expressly stated
Explanation: Companies can charge interest on calls in arrears at the rate mentioned in the Articles of Association. If the Articles follow Table F (model Articles under Companies Act 2013), the maximum rate is 10% p.a. on the amount in arrears.

QuestionText: Which of the following appears under 'Shareholders' Funds' in a company's balance sheet?
Options: A) Share capital and Reserves & Surplus
C) Trade payables and accrued expenses
Explanation: Shareholders' Funds (Equity) in the balance sheet comprises: Share Capital (equity and preference) and Reserves & Surplus (including retained earnings, Securities Premium, General Reserve, Capital Reserve etc.). Loans and payables are liabilities.

QuestionText: When fully paid shares are forfeited, the entry includes credit to:
Options: A) Share Forfeiture Account with full amount paid
Explanation: When fully paid shares are forfeited (e.g., for non-payment of some dues), Share Capital is debited with called-up value and Share Forfeiture Account is credited with the full amount paid up (since no calls are outstanding, the entire paid amount is forfeited).

QuestionText: In which section of the balance sheet are long-term borrowings (like debentures) shown?
Explanation: Long-term borrowings including secured debentures, term loans, and other long-term obligations (repayable after 12 months) are classified as Non-current Liabilities in the balance sheet as per Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013.

QuestionText: A company allots shares to an applicant who applied for 500 shares but receives only 400. The excess application money is:
Explanation: When an applicant receives fewer shares than applied for, excess application money is first adjusted against allotment money due. If any balance remains after meeting allotment, it is adjusted against calls or refunded.

QuestionText: The accounting entry when a company redeems debentures by purchasing from open market at a price below face value is:
Options: A) Debit Own Debentures Account at cost; gain transferred to Capital Reserve
B) Debit Debentures at face value; Credit Bank at face value
C) Debit Capital Reserve; Credit Debenture Account
D) No profit or loss recognised
Explanation: When debentures are purchased from the open market below face value: Own Debentures Account is debited at cost (purchase price). On cancellation, Debentures Account is debited at face value, Own Debentures credited at cost, and the profit (face value minus cost) is credited to Capital Reserve.

QuestionText: Participating preference shares entitle holders to:
Options: A) Share in surplus profits after equity dividend
C) Voting rights on all matters
D) Priority in redemption over secured creditors
Explanation: Participating preference shares give holders two benefits: (1) a fixed preferential dividend, and (2) the right to participate in surplus profits that remain after a specified dividend has been paid to equity shareholders.

QuestionText: Financial statements of companies under the Companies Act 2013 must be prepared following:
Options: A) Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) or AS as applicable
D) Company's own accounting policy without any standard
Explanation: Indian companies prepare financial statements following either Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS, converged with IFRS) for larger companies or older AS (Accounting Standards) issued by ICAI, as applicable based on the company's size and listing status.

QuestionText: The rate of interest on debentures is:
Options: A) Fixed and payable regardless of profits
B) Variable based on company profits
C) Decided each year by shareholders
D) Same as dividend rate on equity shares
Explanation: Debentures carry a fixed rate of interest stated on the debenture certificate. This interest must be paid regardless of whether the company has made a profit or loss. It is a charge against profits (not an appropriation like dividends).

QuestionText: Preliminary expenses of a company are shown in the balance sheet as:
Options: A) Under Other Non-current Assets (to be written off)
Explanation: Preliminary expenses (formation costs) are intangible assets and are shown under 'Other Non-current Assets' and written off over a period. They may be written off against Securities Premium Reserve or charged to Statement of P&L annually.
